unit.title: Communities and Maps Around the World

contentBlocks.text: You've learned what a map is. Today: practice actually reading the small pictures, called symbols, that maps use to show real things.

Maps use small symbols to represent real things — a small tree symbol might mean a park or forest, a small square might mean a building, a blue line might mean a river. The map's key (or legend) tells you what each symbol means, so you don't have to guess. Look at a real map's key (or the symbols listed on your worksheet) and match each symbol to what it represents.
You just practiced a real map-reading skill: using a key to understand symbols! Tomorrow we'll use a map to find land and water.

objectives: Explain that map symbols represent real things, and a key tells you what each symbol means
Match at least three map symbols to what they represent
materialsNeeded: A real map with a key/legend (or printed map symbols)
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review what a map is from last week.
2. Introduce map symbols and the key/legend, using tree/building/river examples.
3. Practice matching symbols to their meanings using a real map or the worksheet examples.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Close by drawing one simple symbol of the child's own for a place near their home.
differentiationTips: Struggling: start with just 2 symbols (tree, building) before adding more
Ready for more: ask the child to design one more symbol for something not yet covered (like a school or a mountain)
A real, physical map (even a simple one) makes this lesson much more concrete than symbols alone
teacherGuide.answerKey: This is a matching activity — check that the child can correctly match at least three symbols (tree=park/forest, square=building, blue line=river) to their meanings.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses the course's 'introduction to reading maps' description, deepening last week's basic map-concept lesson into an actual applied map-reading skill.
